arXiv:2610.25447v1 [cs.LG] 18 Oct 2026

Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning

Tomer Garber Affiliation: Faculty of Engineering, Bar-Ilan University, Ramat Gan, Israel Affiliation: Red Hat    Tom Tirer Affiliation: Faculty of Engineering, Bar-Ilan University, Ramat Gan, Israel
Abstract

Masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) generate text by iteratively unmasking tokens with bidirectional context. As these models reach real-world deployment, machine unlearning becomes essential. This process aims to remove the influence of a designated ‘forget set’ without retraining from scratch, so that sensitive, copyrighted, or restricted content can no longer be elicited while preserving retained capabilities. Masked Diffusion Unlearning (MDU) is the first publicly available unlearning method customized for these models: it tunes the model pθp_{\theta} to match a frozen prompt-masked anchor panchorp_{\mathrm{anchor}} on the forget set by minimizing the anchor-last divergence KL(pθ∥panchor)\mathrm{KL}\bigl(p_{\theta}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{anchor}}\bigr). We identify two failure modes of MDU. First, random answer masking can leave key forget tokens visible to the anchor even when the question is fully masked. Second, at a memorized (near-one-hot) prediction, the anchor-last logit gradient vanishes while the anchor-first divergence KL(panchor∥pθ)\mathrm{KL}\bigl(p_{\mathrm{anchor}}\,\|\,p_{\theta}\bigr) logit gradient does not. As a result, MDU training stalls on the tokens we most need to forget. Backed by theoretical and empirical analyses, we propose Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning (EMDU): anchor-first KL divergence toward a frozen anchor whose entire answer span is masked. On TOFU and RWKU benchmarks using LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B, our EMDU matches or exceeds the forgetting of MDU and adapted AR baselines, while better preserving retain utility.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) trained on web-scale corpora inevitably memorize sensitive personal information, copyrighted material, and private facts. Machine unlearning (Cao & Yang, 2015; Bourtoule et al., 2021) addresses the urgent need to remove designated training data from a deployed model so that forget-set information can no longer be elicited, while preserving performance on retain data. While unlearning in autoregressive (AR) models has matured via gradient ascent (Jang et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2024), preference optimization (Rafailov et al., 2023), and bounded and reweighted objectives (Zhang et al., 2024a; Fan et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025), with dedicated benchmarks (Maini et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2025) and unified evaluation suites (Dorna et al., 2025), extending these concepts to alternative generative paradigms presents distinct challenges. In particular, AR unlearning objectives operate on a single, well-defined next-token log-likelihood, whereas MDLMs train and generate over randomly masked positions and timesteps with no fixed unmasking order; porting such an objective therefore means choosing how to mask and sample for it, a choice that can leave forgotten content recoverable through masking patterns the objective was never defined over. While concept erasure in continuous image diffusion models (Gandikota et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024b) has demonstrated the feasibility of altering denoising trajectories, generative unlearning for discrete text diffusion remains under-explored.

The emergence of Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) (Austin et al., 2021; Lou et al., 2024; Sahoo et al., 2024)—such as LLaDA (Nie et al., 2025) and Dream (Ye et al., 2025)—presents a fundamental shift in text generation. By iteratively denoising sequences of masked tokens via bidirectional context rather than left-to-right prediction, MDLMs achieve strong generative performance and global sequence coherence. As these architectures scale to frontier capabilities (Bie et al., 2025; Inception Labs et al., 2025), ensuring safety and unlearning becomes critical.

Recently, Lee et al. (2026) introduced Masked Diffusion Unlearning (MDU), the first publicly available unlearning framework tailored for MDLMs. It aligns the model’s output on a forget set, pθ(⋅∣x,yt)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{t}), with a prompt-masked unconditional anchor, panchor(⋅∣∅,yt)p_{\mathrm{anchor}}(\cdot\mid\emptyset,y_{t}), scaled by a temperature hyperparameter τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1], via the anchor-last divergence KL(pθ∥panchor)\mathrm{KL}\bigl(p_{\theta}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{anchor}}\bigr). This term is combined with a standard cross-entropy loss on a retain set when available. However, we identify two critical limitations of MDU, which we will elaborate on in this paper: (i) Knowledge leakage: Anchor-last KL pulls pθp_{\theta} toward the diffuse masked anchor by matching the model’s aggregate output distribution rather than directly suppressing the probability of ‘forget tokens’, so sensitive tokens remain recoverable within the resulting noisy generation trajectories even at the anchor’s most diffuse setting (Figure 1); moreover, under random partial masking, unmasked answer tokens can remain visible to the anchor’s own null-context forward pass, so its “unconditional” prediction may still concentrate on the sensitive part of the answer; and (ii) Vanishing ‘forget gradient’: at a memorized (near-one-hot) masked-token prediction, the anchor-last KL’s gradient vanishes while the anchor-first KL’s gradient does not; as a result, under finite-step training (and due to practical nonconvexity, even non-finite), MDU learning stalls exactly on the tokens we most need to forget.

We ask whether the choice of divergence direction, not just the anchor (as suggested in Lee et al. (2026)), is the primary lever for forgetting quality in MDLMs. A second, orthogonal design choice is how the anchor is constructed: under random partial masking, unmasked answer tokens can remain visible to the null-context model, so the unconditional prediction may still concentrate on the forget answer; masking the entire answer span removes that cue. We propose Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning (EMDU), which replaces the anchor-last objective with the anchor-first divergence KL(panchor∥pθ)\mathrm{KL}\bigl(p_{\mathrm{anchor}}\,\|\,p_{\theta}\bigr) and fully masks target answer spans when forming the anchor. Empirically, the unlearned model typically abstains on forget queries by emitting empty (EOS-only) completions rather than fluent paraphrases of the sensitive fact. An empty completion is a safer output mode for unlearning: emitting no tokens is auditable and cannot itself leak partial or hallucinated forget-set content, whereas a long incoherent answer can still include leaks (see MDU generations with τ=0\tau=0 in Figure 1) and a fluent paraphrase risks either regurgitating the original fact or confidently asserting a plausible-sounding wrong one, which is harder to detect and arguably worse for a downstream user, especially in critical applications (see MDU generations with τ=1\tau=1 in Figure 2).

Our key Contributions:

  • •

    We introduce EMDU, a new unlearning method that combines anchor-first KL with full answer-span masking, achieving stronger forgetting and superior retain-set utility over MDU, as well as over prominent methods adapted from AR LLMs to MDLM, on TOFU and RWKU benchmarks with LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B.

  • •

    We theoretically establish that the anchor-last gradient vanishes on memorized forget tokens (and can be small also in a large area around them, making it hard to escape them) while the anchor-first gradient does not. We support this limitation with experiments on real data.

  • •

    We will open-source our project and release (upon acceptance): the models after supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on TOFU (no such models are currently available), EMDU checkpoints for LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B on TOFU and RWKU, and full evaluation scripts.

2 Background and Related Work

2.1 Machine Unlearning

Problem formulation. Given a model MM pre-trained on 𝒟=𝒟f∪𝒟r\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}_{f}\cup\mathcal{D}_{r}, where 𝒟f\mathcal{D}_{f} denotes the forget set (e.g., sensitive personal data or copyrighted text) and 𝒟r\mathcal{D}_{r} the retain set, machine unlearning produces an updated checkpoint M∗M^{*} satisfying two competing objectives: (i) forgetting: M∗M^{*} should no longer reveal information from 𝒟f\mathcal{D}_{f}; and (ii) retention: M∗M^{*} should preserve model performance on 𝒟r\mathcal{D}_{r} and standard downstream tasks.

Unlearning methods. Early approaches established gradient ascent (GA) on 𝒟f\mathcal{D}_{f} as a baseline (Jang et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2024), though unconstrained GA causes catastrophic collapse on general capability. Subsequent work addresses stability: Gradient Difference (GD) (Maini et al., 2024) balances GA on 𝒟f\mathcal{D}_{f} with gradient descent on 𝒟r\mathcal{D}_{r}; Negative Preference Optimization (NPO) (Zhang et al., 2024a) and SimNPO (Fan et al., 2025) reframe forgetting as bounded preference optimization; Weighted Gradient Ascent (WGA) (Wang et al., 2025) applies token-level weighting to limit collapse; and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023) is adapted into an unlearning baseline that prefers a refusal (Zhang et al., 2024a) or a perturbed answer over the forget response. Dedicated benchmarks such as TOFU (Maini et al., 2024), RWKU (Jin et al., 2024), WMDP (Li et al., 2024), and MUSE (Shi et al., 2025) probe different unlearning settings, and unified evaluation suites such as OpenUnlearning (Dorna et al., 2025) standardize methods and metrics across them. All of the above methods were originally designed for autoregressive LLMs. As mentioned above, recently, Lee et al. (2026) introduced Masked Diffusion Unlearning (MDU), the first publicly available unlearning method designed for MDLMs, which we describe in detail in §2.3.

Unlearning in image diffusion models. A parallel line of work targets concept erasure in continuous image diffusion models (e.g., ESD (Gandikota et al., 2023), AdvUnlearn (Zhang et al., 2024b)). These methods optimize continuous noise trajectories to alter visual outputs. Because they rely on Gaussian noise schedules over continuous latents, they do not directly transfer to the discrete absorbing-state masking process of text-based MDLMs.

Adversarial robustness. Concurrent work by Zhang et al. (2026) (made publicly available after MDU (Lee et al., 2026)) finds that unlearning performance in MDLMs is sensitive to generation length and denoising steps. It proposes adversarial RL, in which a separate LLM generates contexts that elicit forgotten knowledge while the MDLM learns, via GRPO, to suppress it.

2.2 Masked Diffusion Language Models

Continuous image diffusion has become the dominant paradigm for high-fidelity image generation, editing, and restoration (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021a; Song et al., 2021b; Meng et al., 2022; Song et al., 2023; Garber & Tirer, 2024; Garber & Tirer, 2025), modeling data as iterative denoising of corrupted inputs. Masked Diffusion Language Models inherit this conceptual foundation for discrete text. Discrete diffusion was formalized by D3PM (Austin et al., 2021) using absorbing-state transitions, and refined by SEDD (Lou et al., 2024) via score-entropy matching. MDLM (Sahoo et al., 2024) simplified this into a substitution-based framework (their SUBS parameterization, which enforces zero probability of predicting [𝙼𝙰𝚂𝙺][\mathtt{MASK}] and carries over already-unmasked tokens unchanged), showing that the continuous-time ELBO reduces to a weighted sum of cross-entropy terms over masked positions. Block Diffusion (Arriola et al., 2025) extends this framework block-wise, interpolating between diffusion and autoregressive generation.

Scaled backbones LLaDA (Nie et al., 2025) and Dream (Ye et al., 2025) extend MDLM’s architecture to multi-billion-parameter instruction models. LLaDA trains a bidirectional Transformer from scratch; Dream initializes from an AR checkpoint to leverage pre-trained LLMs. Both adopt the following standard MDLM corrupting process. Consider the vocabulary 𝒱={1,…,V}\mathcal{V}=\{1,\ldots,V\}. At timepoint t∼U(0,1]t\sim U(0,1], each response token y(i)y^{(i)} (word from the vocabulary) is independently masked with probability tt, yielding noisy sequence yty_{t} with masked-position set ℳt={i∣yt(i)=[𝙼𝙰𝚂𝙺]}\mathcal{M}_{t}=\{i\mid y_{t}^{(i)}=[\mathtt{MASK}]\}. The model pθ​(y(i)∣x,yt)p_{\theta}(y^{(i)}\mid x,y_{t}) uses full bidirectional context to reconstruct masked tokens.

We present the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) form of this ELBO, where the prompt xx is held fixed and only the response yy is masked (unlike pretraining, which masks the entire sequence with no prompt held out). This SFT objective essentially has the following cross-entropy loss form, used throughout this paper for the base SFT and for the retain term:

ℒCE(x,y,t;θ)=−1t∑i∈ℳtlogpθ(y(i)∣x,yt),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(x,y,t;\theta)\;=\;-\frac{1}{t}\sum\nolimits_{i\in\mathcal{M}_{t}}\log p_{\theta}(y^{(i)}\mid x,y_{t}), (1)

where 1/t1/t, the ELBO weight under this linear schedule, reweights token positions according to masking density. Lastly, note that the same model can be run conditionally on a prompt xx, written pθ(⋅|x,yt)p_{\theta}(\cdot|x,y_{t}), or unconditionally by replacing the prompt with masks ∅\emptyset, written pθ(⋅|∅,yt)p_{\theta}(\cdot|\emptyset,y_{t}). This is the discrete analogue of classifier-free guidance’s split (Ho & Salimans, 2022), where the model supports both conditional and unconditional denoising.

2.3 Unlearning for Masked Diffusion Models

MDU. Masked Diffusion Unlearning (MDU) is the first publicly available unlearning training objective tailored for MDLMs (Lee et al., 2026). Denote the MDLM parameters before the unlearning procedure by pθ0p_{\theta_{0}}. For a forget prompt-response pair (x,y)∈𝒟f(x,y)\in\mathcal{D}_{f}, MDU samples timepoint tt and noisy version of the response yty_{t}, constructing a prompt-masked anchor by evaluating the pre-unlearning model pθ0p_{\theta_{0}} on unprompted context (∅,yt)(\emptyset,y_{t})—the unconditional denoiser mentioned in §2.2—with temperature scaling τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1]: panchor=softmax(τlogpθ0(⋅|∅,yt))p_{\mathrm{anchor}}=\mathrm{softmax}(\tau\log p_{\theta_{0}}(\cdot|\emptyset,y_{t})), where the softmax is computed per token. The model being optimized is computed by the conditional denoiser: pθ=pθ(⋅|x,yt)p_{\theta}=p_{\theta}(\cdot|x,y_{t}). Both are compared only at the masked answer positions ℳt={i∣yt(i)=[𝙼𝙰𝚂𝙺]}\mathcal{M}_{t}=\{i\mid y_{t}^{(i)}=[\mathtt{MASK}]\} (as in Eq. (1)): the forget KL is applied only at i∈ℳti\in\mathcal{M}_{t}, averaged uniformly over |ℳt||\mathcal{M}_{t}|.

KL orientation. We write anchor-last for KL(pθ∥panchor)\mathrm{KL}(p_{\theta}\|p_{\mathrm{anchor}}) and anchor-first for KL(panchor∥pθ)\mathrm{KL}(p_{\mathrm{anchor}}\|p_{\theta}). MDU calls the anchor-last direction “forward KL”—the opposite of the widespread convention in variational inference and knowledge distillation, where “forward” usually denotes KL(target∥model)\mathrm{KL}(\mathrm{target}\|\mathrm{model}) (Minka, 2005; Wu et al., 2025). We use anchor-last / anchor-first throughout to keep the argument order unambiguous. MDU minimizes the anchor-last divergence:

ℒAL(x,y,t;θ)=KL(pθ∥panchor)=∑k=1Vpθ,klogpθ,kpanchor,k.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AL}}(x,y,t;\theta)\;=\;\mathrm{KL}(p_{\theta}\,\|\,p_{\mathrm{anchor}})\;=\;\sum\nolimits_{k=1}^{V}p_{\theta,k}\log\frac{p_{\theta,k}}{p_{\mathrm{anchor},k}}. (2)

This is a per-token quantity, computed at each masked answer position i∈ℳti\in\mathcal{M}_{t} and averaged uniformly over |ℳt||\mathcal{M}_{t}|.

Setting τ=0\tau=0 collapses panchorp_{\mathrm{anchor}} to a uniform distribution (maximum-entropy noise); τ=1\tau=1 matches unconditional model predictions. MDU quantifies this continuum with LLaDA pseudo-perplexity on TOFU (Table 7 in their paper): forget PPL is extremely high at low τ\tau and falls toward base as τ\tau increases, while retain/RA/WF PPL stay near the base model. Figure 1 further shows that low-τ\tau generations can still surface forget tokens despite being incoherent, and Figure 2 shows that at τ=1\tau{=}1 generations become fluent but can be confidently wrong or leak the correct answer. To preserve utility, MDU combines this forget objective, 𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟f,t​[ℒAL​(x,y,t,θ)]\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{f},t}[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AL}}(x,y,t;\theta)], with a standard cross-entropy retain loss, 𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟r,t​[ℒCE​(x,y,t,θ)]\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{r},t}[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(x,y,t;\theta)], computed on 𝒟r\mathcal{D}_{r} and weighted by a scalar α\alpha.

Under the usual variational inference notation, where pp is fixed and qq is optimized, KL(p∥q)\mathrm{KL}(p\|q) (anchor-first) is described as mass-covering and KL(q∥p)\mathrm{KL}(q\|p) (anchor-last) as mode-seeking (Minka, 2005). This heuristic rests on p,qp,q being continuous, unimodal densities fit from samples, and is known not to transfer cleanly to LLM knowledge distillation, where the fitted distributions are instead discrete, high-dimensional categorical distributions (Wu et al., 2025). Moreover, both orientations are strictly convex in qq and share the same unique minimizer q=pq=p (Cover & Thomas, 2006), so mode-seeking/mass-covering cannot explain why anchor-first outperforms anchor-last in practice, as will be shown in this paper. We argue that the reason is dynamical: §4 shows that for a near-one-hot SFT initialization on a forget set’s token, anchor-last’s gradient vanishes early in training while anchor-first’s gradient does not. This is exacerbated by practical nonconvexity: in practice, more iterations do not resolve this limitation.

3 EMDU: Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning

In this section, we propose our Enhanced Masked Diffusion Unlearning (EMDU) method. EMDU keeps MDU’s frozen prompt-masked anchor and temperature τ\tau and changes two ingredients: the forget divergence, and how the anchor’s answer span is corrupted. §4 analyzes the divergence; this section specifies the procedure. Empirically, the resulting model often abstains on forget queries by emitting empty (EOS-only) completions which, as discussed in §1, is a safe unlearning output.

3.1 Anchor-first forget loss

Let pθp_{\theta} be the optimized model at a masked response position and panchorp_{\mathrm{anchor}} the frozen prompt-masked anchor, as in §2.3. MDU minimizes the anchor-last KL, EMDU instead minimizes the anchor-first KL:

ℒAF(x,y,t;θ)=KL(panchor∥pθ)=∑k=1Vpanchor,klogpanchor,kpθ,k.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AF}}(x,y,t;\theta)\;=\;\mathrm{KL}(p_{\mathrm{anchor}}\,\|\,p_{\theta})\;=\;\sum\nolimits_{k=1}^{V}p_{\mathrm{anchor},k}\log\frac{p_{\mathrm{anchor},k}}{p_{\theta,k}}. (3)

This uses the same ℳt\mathcal{M}_{t} masking and uniform averaging as MDU’s forget loss (Equation (2)). Gradient dynamics of the two KL directions are compared in §4, showing that anchor-first KL better fits unlearning from confidently memorized (near-one-hot) predictions.

3.2 Full answer-span masking

Under MDU, the optimized model and frozen anchor share the same randomly masked answer yty_{t}, where each token is masked independently with probability tt. The optimized model is conditioned on the prompt (x,yt)(x,y_{t}); the anchor is evaluated on the prompt-masked pair (∅,yt)(\emptyset,y_{t}). Unmasked forget tokens therefore remain as bidirectional context for the frozen model. The KL is applied only on masked positions—there is no loss on the visible ones in yty_{t}—but those survivors shape panchorp_{\mathrm{anchor}} at the masked slots (since yty_{t} is inputted to panchorp_{\mathrm{anchor}}). Therefore, the target that the optimized model is pulled toward can still concentrate on the forget answer. Figure 3 illustrates the failure: a few surviving answer tokens can cue the sensitive span in the anchor’s masked-position predictions.

EMDU thus applies full answer-span masking (FAM) on the anchor forward only: every answer position is replaced by [𝙼𝙰𝚂𝙺][\mathtt{MASK}] when forming panchorp_{\mathrm{anchor}}, while the optimized model continues to see randomly masked yty_{t}. FAM changes the anchor input, and does not affect the computation of pθp_{\theta}.

3.3 Training objective

The full objective is anchor-first KL on forget examples plus the same retain cross-entropy weighted by α\alpha as MDU:

ℒEMDU​(θ)=𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟f,t​[ℒAF​(x,y,t,θ)]+α​𝔼(x,y)∼𝒟r,t​[ℒCE​(x,y,t,θ)].\mathcal{L}_{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{EMDU}}}(\theta)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{f},t}[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AF}}(x,y,t;\theta)]\;+\;\alpha\,\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{r},t}[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(x,y,t;\theta)]. (4)

Every training step draws a forget minibatch together with an independently sampled, same-size retain minibatch; the two terms are computed on their respective minibatches and summed before one parameter update (Algorithm 1, Appendix C). The frozen anchor still uses temperature τ\tau. As with MDU, the retain term applies only when the benchmark provides a retain set; for benchmarks without one (e.g., RWKU), we drop α​ℒCE\alpha\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}.

4 Method Analysis

We compare the anchor-last and anchor-first KL forget losses at a single masked response position using the same frozen prompt-masked anchor. Since the losses are summed over the masked set ℳt\mathcal{M}_{t} with the uniform 1/|ℳt|1/|\mathcal{M}_{t}| weights, the conclusions we reach apply tokenwise.

Consider the vocabulary 𝒱={1,…,V}\mathcal{V}=\{1,\ldots,V\}. We use z∈ℝVz\in\mathbb{R}^{V} to denote the logits of the optimized model and q=softmax⁡(z)∈ΔV−1q=\mathrm{softmax}(z)\in\Delta^{V-1} to denote pθp_{\theta}. We use p∈ΔV−1p\in\Delta^{V-1} to denote the anchor panchorp_{\mathrm{anchor}}, potentially after temperature scaling with τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1]. For τ=0\tau=0, pp is uniform. With a slight abuse of notation, let

ℒAL(z)=KL(q∥p)=∑k=1Vqklogqkpk,ℒAF(z)=KL(p∥q)=∑k=1Vpklogpkqk.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AL}}(z)\;=\;\mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p)\;=\;\sum\nolimits_{k=1}^{V}q_{k}\log\frac{q_{k}}{p_{k}},\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AF}}(z)\;=\;\mathrm{KL}(p\,\|\,q)\;=\;\sum\nolimits_{k=1}^{V}p_{k}\log\frac{p_{k}}{q_{k}}. (5)

Recall that only qq depends on zz. Both maps q↦KL(q∥p)q\mapsto\mathrm{KL}(q\|p) and q↦KL(p∥q)q\mapsto\mathrm{KL}(p\|q) are strictly convex and uniquely minimized at q=pq=p by Gibbs’ inequality (Cover & Thomas, 2006). Yet, below we establish a distinction in gradient dynamics from a near-one-hot (SFT) initialization. Proofs are in Appendix A.

4.1 Gradient saturation at memorized predictions

We first state the gradients of ℒAL​(z)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AL}}(z) and ℒAF​(z)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AF}}(z), with ⊙\odot denoting the Hadamard product.

Proposition 1 (Logit gradients).

For q=softmax⁡(z)q=\mathrm{softmax}(z) and pp constant with respect to zz,

∇zℒAL=q⊙(logqp−KL(q∥p) 1),∇zℒAF=q−p.\displaystyle\nabla_{z}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AL}}=q\odot\Bigl(\log\frac{q}{p}-\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)\,\mathbf{1}\Bigr),\qquad\nabla_{z}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AF}}=q-p. (6)

Both gradients lie in the tangent space {v:∑kvk=0}\{\,v:\sum_{k}v_{k}=0\,\}, as required by shift invariance of softmax.

The anchor-first gradient ∇zℒAF\nabla_{z}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AF}} equals the standard softmax cross-entropy gradient toward the frozen target pp: gradient descent decreases zjz_{j} wherever qj>pjq_{j}>p_{j} and increases zjz_{j} wherever qj<pjq_{j}<p_{j}, with force equal to the probability gap. The anchor-last gradient ∇zℒAL\nabla_{z}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AL}} is weighted by qq itself. We will show that coordinates where the model is very confident contribute a vanishing update regardless of pp.

Let e(j)∈ΔV−1e^{(j)}\in\Delta^{V-1} denote the jj-th vertex (the one-hot vector on token jj). A highly memorized masked-token prediction corresponds to an optimized-model prediction qq near e(j)e^{(j)}. This is exactly the regime of interest: a memorized position starts at SFT initialization with q≈e(j)q\approx e^{(j)}, and the question is how quickly the forget loss can move it away. Our main technical contribution is Theorem 2 below, which is stated for any qq close to e(j)e^{(j)} (small ε=1−qj\varepsilon=1-q_{j}), not only in the limit, so that it applies throughout training as the model sits near (and is meant to escape from) the memorized vertex, not only at convergence.

Theorem 2 (Anchor-last gradient rate).

Fix p∈ΔV−1p\in\Delta^{V-1} with pk>0p_{k}>0 for all kk, and j∈𝒱j\in\mathcal{V}. For q=softmax⁡(z)∈ΔV−1q=\mathrm{softmax}(z)\in\Delta^{V-1} with ε:=1−qj∈(0,1/2]\varepsilon:=1-q_{j}\in(0,1/2], we have ∥∇zKL(q∥p)∥1≤C(p)εlogVε\bigl\|\nabla_{z}\mathrm{KL}(q\|p)\bigr\|_{1}\;\leq\;C(p)\,\varepsilon\log\frac{V}{\varepsilon}, for a constant C⁡(p)<∞C(p)<\infty depending only on pp.

We next state the values of the divergences and their gradients as qq approaches e(j)e^{(j)} (using Theorem 2 for the anchor-last gradient).

Proposition 3 (Anchor-last KL saturates; anchor-first does not).

Fix p∈ΔV−1p\in\Delta^{V-1} with pk>0p_{k}>0 for all kk and an index j∈𝒱j\in\mathcal{V} with pj<1p_{j}<1. As q=softmax⁡(z)→e(j)q=\mathrm{softmax}(z)\to e^{(j)}, we have

ℒAL→−log⁡pj<∞,ℒAF→+∞.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AL}}\;\to\;-\log p_{j}\;<\;\infty,\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AF}}\;\to\;+\infty. (7)
∇zℒAL→ 0,∇zℒAF→e(j)−p≠ 0.\nabla_{z}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AL}}\;\to\;0,\qquad\nabla_{z}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AF}}\;\to\;e^{(j)}-p\;\neq\;0. (8)

In particular, along the ray z⁡(s)=s​e(j)z(s)=s\,e^{(j)} as s→+∞s\to+\infty (so q⁡(s)→e(j)q(s)\to e^{(j)}),

ℒAF(s)=(1−pj)s+O(1),(∇zℒAL)j(s)=O(sexp(−s))(s→+∞).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AF}}(s)\;=\;(1-p_{j})\,s+O(1),\qquad\bigl(\nabla_{z}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AL}}\bigr)_{j}(s)\;=O(s\exp(-s))\qquad(s\to+\infty). (9)

By Equation (9), anchor-first KL grows linearly in the forget token logit while anchor-last plateaus—anchor-first is “more eager” to move logits away from a memorized one-hot prediction, both in the limit and at finite points along the ray (z⁡(s)z(s) with large enough ss). The anchor-first gradient limit is in fact nonzero on every coordinate, (∇zℒAF)k→δk​j−pk(\nabla_{z}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AF}})_{k}\to\delta_{kj}-p_{k}: off-answer logits keep a force −pk-p_{k}, continually reallocating tail mass toward the anchor. The same holds for any target with pj<1p_{j}<1.

Theorem 2’s O⁡(ε​log⁡(1/ε))O(\varepsilon\log(1/\varepsilon)) rate makes this gap quantitative: since (∇zℒAL)j→0(\nabla_{z}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AL}})_{j}\to 0 while (∇zℒAF)j→1−pj>0(\nabla_{z}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AF}})_{j}\to 1-p_{j}>0, at small enough ε\varepsilon, the anchor-first jj-force dominates for every leftover-mass shape on 𝒱∖{j}\mathcal{V}\setminus\{j\} and every interior anchor pp. Equation (9) shows that along the ray, escaping a memorized token with −∇zℒAL-\nabla_{z}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AL}} is not easy: for sufficiently large s1s_{1}, even if s1≪s2s_{1}\ll s_{2} (implying that q⁡(s1)q(s_{1}) is further from e(j)e^{(j)} than q⁡(s2)q(s_{2})) the gradients of both logits z⁡(s1)z(s_{1}) and z⁡(s2)z(s_{2}) are nearly equal to zero.

Additional analysis, in a simplified setup, of the range of probabilities where ∇zℒAF\nabla_{z}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AF}} is dominant is presented in Appendix B. Below, we empirically validate on real data the distinction between the KL modes in escaping confident forget tokens.

4.2 Escaping memorized forget tokens

To support our theoretical analysis, we study the presence of memorized tokens and the dynamics of escaping them on LLaDA-8B-Instruct model and TOFU dataset (forget10 with retain90). Table 1 presents the results for training with anchor-last and anchor-first KL with identical hyperparameters and τ=1\tau=1, differing only in the KL direction (FAM is off for both). At SFT initialization, 92.2%92.2\% of 7,2117{,}211 probed positions satisfy qy>0.9q_{y}>0.9 and 77.2%77.2\% satisfy qy>0.99q_{y}>0.99. This demonstrates that after SFT many forget tokens are near a vertex of the probability simplex. After nine epochs of anchor-last unlearning, the high-confidence mass has only fallen to 35.5%35.5\% / 18.8%18.8\% with a trend that flattens by epoch 66. Anchor-first drops the same fractions to 10.0%10.0\% / 1.2%1.2\% by the end of epoch 44. Mean qyq_{y} reflects the same split (0.550.55 for anchor-last vs. 0.370.37 for anchor-first at epoch 99), confirming that residual knowledge under anchor-last stems from persistent, high-confidence memorized positions.

Note that while our theory identifies the weakness of anchor-last compared to anchor-first in finite-time optimization (we present a gradient-based result, while eventually both terms have the same minimizer), more training epochs do not close the gap and the measured fractions reached plateaus at different levels, presumably due to the nonconvexity of the model. The dynamics shown here motivate using the anchor-first divergence for escaping memorized forget-token predictions.

5 Experiments

TOFU setup and metrics. We fine-tune LLaDA-8B-Instruct and Dream-7B-Instruct on TOFU (Maini et al., 2024) full to obtain Base SFT checkpoints, using the fine-tuning hyperparameters suggested by MDU (Appendix D.2), then unlearn on forget10 with retain90. All training and evaluation runs use NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs. Unless otherwise noted, TOFU generations use 128128 denoising steps and 128128 output tokens (the MDLM answer canvas), matching the MDU evaluation protocol. Following MDU, we report Rouge-L recall (rL) and answer probability (pp) on Forget, Retain, Real Authors (RA), and World Facts (WF). Rouge-L (rL) is Rouge-L recall between the generated string and the reference answer. Answer probability pp is defined in Appendix D.1.

RWKU setup and metrics. We consider the first 10 subjects (out of 200 subjects total) of the RWKU (Jin et al., 2024) dataset, the same subset used by MDU. We match MDU’s metrics: F-L1/N-L1 (knowledge memorization), F-L2/N-L2 (knowledge manipulation via paraphrased/reasoning QA), and F-L3 (robustness to adversarial-attack prompts)—all Rouge-L recall, following RWKU’s official protocol—plus MMLU, TruQA, and TriQA. Unlike TOFU, RWKU does not require fine-tuning: we unlearn each subject independently from the off-the-shelf Instruct checkpoint, using that subject’s official RWKU forget pairs (582582 prompt–response biographies per entity) and no retain set. Base rows are macro averages over those ten subjects (mean of per-subject means for forget and neighbor; TruQA / TriQA likewise over ten subjects; MMLU is the shared utility suite).

Examined Methods. We compare to the same baselines from Lee et al. (2026) adapted from AR to MDLM: GA, GD, NPO, SimNPO, WGA, DPO with the addition of MDU, each tuned over learning rate and training length (Appendix D). GD is not relevant for RWKU, which does not have a designated retain set. For MDU and EMDU, we set τ=1\tau=1. In Appendix F (Figure 7) we sweep τ\tau for both methods and show that: 1) our EMDU with τ=1\tau=1 outperforms MDU with any τ\tau examined, and 2) our EMDU is usually stable with respect to τ\tau.

5.1 TOFU and RWKU results

Ablation on TOFU. Table 2 ablates AF and FAM. On both backbones, AF alone and FAM alone each push Forget rL to or near zero, but FAM alone pays a large Retain (LLaDA) or RA/WF (Dream) cost; only their combination, EMDU, does well on every metric. AF alone also forgets more than AL alone on both backbones, while FAM removes anchor-side leakage. This matches the theoretical prediction of §4: unlike AL, whose gradient vanishes on confident (near-one-hot) forget predictions, AF’s gradient does not, letting it escape memorized answers more effectively even without FAM. It also improves Retain over AL alone on both backbones. EosSFT, a supervised baseline for this ablation study, trains the model to answer forget queries with EOS tokens using the same SFT cross-entropy objective (Equation 1) as Base SFT and the retain term, but with an EOS-only target instead of the real answer. It only partially suppresses Forget and costs Retain, RA, and WF.

TOFU results. The results are presented in Table 3. Our MDU numbers differ from those reported by Lee et al. (2026); we obtain them by running their official code under their suggested configuration. They did not release Base SFT or unlearned checkpoints, and the released code was only partial, so we could not reproduce their reported numbers from artifacts alone (details in Appendix E.1). Adapted AR baselines fail in different ways: GA and GD damage utility, DPO under-forgets, and NPO, SimNPO and WGA forget most strongly among them but still have lower Retain than EMDU on both backbones. MDU substantially reduces Forget but has the weakest (LLaDA) or second-weakest (Dream) Retain of all baselines. EMDU has the lowest Forget rL on both backbones, a Forget pp similar to the best, and the highest Retain, with RA and WF remaining competitive or best across the two backbones. Figure 7 (Appendix F) sweeps τ\tau for MDU versus EMDU, showing that EMDU with τ=1\tau=1 outperforms MDU with any τ\tau we examined.

RWKU results. The results are presented in Table 4. The AR-adapted baselines cluster together on Forget, behind EMDU, with only modest differences in how much Neighbor and Utility each trades away for that residual forgetting. MDU reaches a lower F-L3 (adversarial-robustness axis) than any of them, but its F-L1 (direct knowledge-memorization) lags behind every baseline, and on Dream several of its Neighbor and Utility scores drop sharply. EMDU forgets most strongly overall on both backbones and best preserves N-L1 on both backbones and N-L2 on LLaDA. It also keeps MMLU and other utility scores best or competitive.

Empty completions. EMDU yields empty (EOS-only) completions on 71.8%71.8\% / 99.0%99.0\% of TOFU forget queries (LLaDA / Dream), with at most 0.5%0.5\% empty on Retain, RA, and WF—i.e., the model typically emits no tokens about the forgotten fact rather than a fluent paraphrase. On RWKU the same pattern holds but less completely: across the three forget sets (F-L1/L2/L3) and both backbones, 3535–60%60\% of queries return an empty response. Because Rouge-L is computed only on the text preceding the first EOS token, we additionally inspected the full generation canvas to check for leakage beyond it: on these empty completions, EOS appears at the very first answer position and every remaining position resolves to EOS as well, with nothing hidden past the truncation point. Appendix G gives concrete examples, on both TOFU and RWKU, where EMDU abstains while every (or nearly every) other evaluated method leaks the forgotten fact, as well as retain-side comparisons.

In deployment, an empty completion can be replaced by a generic “I don’t know” response without changing the unlearned weights. A named-entity recognizer (Lample et al., 2016) can further extract the question’s subject and template a specific response—for example, mapping “Can you specify the birthplace of author Ji-Yeon Park?” to “I don’t have information about Ji-Yeon Park.”

5.2 Robustness

Generation robustness. The concurrent work of Zhang et al. (2026) shows that unlearning effectiveness for diffusion language models is highly sensitive to generation hyperparameters, particularly output length and the number of denoising steps. We therefore re-evaluate checkpoints across all six output-length/denoising-step combinations they use; full numbers are in Table 7 (Appendix F). EMDU keeps near-zero Forget across this range on both backbones, with Retain / RA / WF declining only mildly, on the order of the SFT baseline’s own sensitivity. MDU is markedly less stable under coarser sampling.

Paraphrased questions. Empty forget completions on the original phrasing do not by themselves show that the fact is gone: a model could still answer a reworded probe. We therefore also evaluate forget10 with TOFU’s official paraphrased questions: Table 8 (Appendix F) shows EMDU’s Forget stays near zero under paraphrase on both backbones, while SFT remains high, so EMDU’s forgetting does not depend on the exact question wording.

Seed variance. The methods in Tables 3 and 4 are trained and evaluated at a single fixed seed, following the practice of Lee et al. (2026), due to limited compute resources. We re-run EMDU’s chosen configurations for TOFU and RWKU with 22 additional independent unlearning seeds per backbone and report mean ±\pm std in Tables 9 and 10 (Appendix F). The resulting spread is small across both datasets and both backbones, and EMDU’s Forget and Retain remain clearly separated from MDU’s single-seed numbers in Table 3 in every seed we ran, showing that its advantage over MDU is not an artifact of the particular seed reported.

6 Conclusions

We presented EMDU: anchor-first KL with full answer-span masking for unlearning in masked diffusion language models. On TOFU, the method strongly reduces the forget-set’s Rouge-L and answer probability while preserving retain and probe utility, and typically abstains with EOS-only canvases on forget queries. Relative to MDU, abstention avoids the gibberish-vs-fluency tradeoff along τ\tau, and the empty canvas can be rendered as a fixed or templated response at deployment time. Future research can explore whether the same gradient-saturation mechanism identified in §4 also explains KL-direction choices in other settings built on the same divergence, such as knowledge distillation and post-training (Chen et al., 2026; Shenfeld et al., 2026).

Appendix A Proofs for Section 4

We write H(p)=−∑k=1VpklogpkH(p)=-\sum_{k=1}^{V}p_{k}\log p_{k} for Shannon entropy (natural log). Throughout, p∈ΔV−1p\in\Delta^{V-1} is fixed with pk>0p_{k}>0 for all kk.

A.1 Proof of Proposition 1

Proof.

First, note that the softmax Jacobian is ∂qk/∂zj=qk​(δk​j−qj)\partial q_{k}/\partial z_{j}=q_{k}(\delta_{kj}-q_{j}), where δk​j\delta_{kj} denotes the Kronecker delta.

For anchor-first KL, ℒAF=−∑kpklogqk+const(p)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AF}}=-\sum_{k}p_{k}\log q_{k}+\mathrm{const}(p). Differentiating log⁡qk\log q_{k} through softmax gives ∂log⁡qk/∂zj=δk​j−qj\partial\log q_{k}/\partial z_{j}=\delta_{kj}-q_{j}, hence

∂ℒAF∂zj=−∑kpk(δk​j−qj)=−pj+qj∑kpk=qj−pj.\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AF}}}{\partial z_{j}}=-\sum_{k}p_{k}(\delta_{kj}-q_{j})=-p_{j}+q_{j}\sum_{k}p_{k}=q_{j}-p_{j}.

For anchor-last KL, ℒAL=∑kqk​(log⁡qk−log⁡pk)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{AL}}=\sum_{k}q_{k}(\log q_{k}-\log p_{k}). The partial with respect to
